Abstract
This research examines the fundamental transformations within the real-estate tenancy laws
in Egypt, a system previously marked by a perpetuity that surpasses the inherent nature of
lease contracts. The study highlights the Supreme Constitutional Court’s role in establishing
temporal and substantive frameworks to restore the balance between landlords and tenants.
The legal reform is characterized by the following pillars:
• The Role of the Judiciary: The Court of Cassation intervened to fill legislative gaps by
applying Article 563 of the Civil Code as a general principle to terminate perpetual lease
contracts.
• The Role of the Legislature: Recent legislative trends, such as Law No. 10 of 2022 and
Law No. 164 of 2025, have introduced gradual rent increases and set a definitive end to
the lease relationship after specific transitional periods.

• Practical Obstacles: Implementation is hindered by the inconsistent performance of
valuation committees, leading to discrepancies in rent increases. Furthermore, new
grounds for the obligatory vacating of leased premises have been established, such as the
tenant owning an alternative property or the premises remaining closed for extended
periods.
In conclusion, the research affirms that Egypt is transitioning away from exceptional
legislation toward the Civil Code. This shift re-establishes the lease contract as a contract
of limited duration, ensuring landlords receive a reasonable return on their real estate
investments while maintaining a social dimension for tenants through transitional periods.
